entities.name: Assembly of Vizille
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Assembly of Vizille, convened on July 21, 1788 at the Château de Vizille near Grenoble — bringing together representatives of the three estates of the Dauphiné province (clergy, nobility, and Third Estate) in defiance of royal prohibition on regional assemblies — is regarded by historians as the 'spark of the French Revolution': the first successful assertion of representative government against royal absolutism, which preceded and directly inspired the Estates-General convened in 1789 that launched the French Revolution.

The Assembly was convened in response to Louis XVI's May 1788 edicts suppressing existing parlements (regional courts with quasi-legislative powers) and centralizing judicial-administrative power in new royal courts. The three estates of Dauphiné, led by the lawyer Antoine Barnave (later a Constituent Assembly leader), the nobleman Mounier, and others, met at the home of Claude Périer — a wealthy merchant — to protest the royal edicts. Crucially, the three estates met and voted jointly rather than separately, prefiguring the key revolutionary demand of the Third Estate in 1789.

The Assembly of Vizille demanded the restoration of the Dauphiné provincial estates, the convocation of the Estates-General (not called since 1614), and the restoration of traditional liberties — all demands that became the opening salvos of the French Revolution. The revolutionary innovation of joint deliberation across the three orders was a direct precursor to the Third Estate's June 1789 decision to constitute itself as the National Assembly. The Vizille meeting thus stands at the very beginning of the constitutional chain that produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Assembly of Vizille — the 1788 provincial assembly that first successfully defied royal absolutism through joint three-estate deliberation, demanded the Estates-General, and established the procedural precedent for the National Assembly — is the direct institutional spark of the French Revolution.
